## The Great French Wine Blight {background-color="#1B4332"}

*Le grand fléau du phylloxéra*

::: {.notes}
Opening story, ~8-9 min total. Hook question, then timeline, then the
mechanism (why European vines had zero resistance), then the
resolution (grafting), then bridge explicitly to "resistance" as
today's theme.
:::

## Paris, late 1800s {.hook}

<!-- TODO: image of a Belle Époque absinthe poster/café scene. -->

> **A cheap, bright-green, wormwood-and-anise spirit becomes the
> drink of a generation — nicknamed the "Green Fairy." Absinthe
> eclipses France's most sacred drink: wine. Why?**
>
> *Un spiritueux vert vif, à base d'absinthe et d'anis, devient la
> boisson d'une génération — surnommée la « fée verte ». L'absinthe
> éclipse la boisson la plus sacrée de France : le vin. Pourquoi ?*

⏳ Think, 45 seconds — talk to your neighbor.

::: {.notes}
Let a few guesses land (cheaper? fashionable? artists?) before the
reveal. All true, but there's a deeper, entirely botanical cause
underneath the fashion story. ~2 min including the reveal below.
:::

## The vines were dying

- In the 1860s, French vineyards began mysteriously wilting and
  dying, vineyard by vineyard, with no known cause
- By the 1880s, an estimated **two-thirds of French vineyards** had
  been destroyed
- Wine became scarce and expensive — ordinary people needed a
  substitute, and absinthe (grain- and herb-based, not grape-based)
  was cheap, strong, and unaffected by the shortage

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is "Le Grand Phylloxéra" - one of the most destructive
plant epidemics in agricultural history.
:::

## The culprit: *Phylloxera*

- A tiny aphid-like insect, **grape phylloxera**
  (*Daktulosphaira vitifoliae*), native to North America
- Accidentally introduced to France around 1863-1865, likely on
  American vine cuttings brought over for research
- Feeds on grapevine **roots**, forming galls that cut off water and
  nutrients — slow, invisible death underground, months before any
  symptom shows above ground

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. The insect is barely visible to the naked eye - part of why
it took years to identify the cause.
:::

## Why was it so devastating?

- American grapevine species (*Vitis* spp.) had coexisted with
  phylloxera for millions of years — many evolved genuine
  **root resistance**
- European wine grapes (*Vitis vinifera*) had **never encountered
  phylloxera** before — zero coevolutionary history, zero resistance
- A naive host meeting a well-adapted enemy for the first time is
  close to a worst-case scenario in chemical ecology

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is the conceptual heart of the story: resistance isn't
a fixed property of a species, it's the product of a long
evolutionary "arms race" with a specific enemy. Remove the shared
history, and the defense often isn't there at all.
:::

## The fix — and it's still used today

- The solution wasn't a pesticide — it was **resistance itself**:
  graft European *Vitis vinifera* vines onto **American rootstock**
- The American roots survive phylloxera; the European vine above the
  graft still produces the same wine
- Nearly every commercial vineyard on Earth today grows on grafted
  American rootstock — a permanent legacy of this one insect

**Bridge to today: this whole week is about exactly what saved the
wine industry — how plants resist being eaten, and what happens when
that resistance is present, absent, or overcome.**

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min close. Explicit bridge into the direct-resistance framework:
American rootstock = constitutive physical/chemical resistance built
over deep evolutionary time; European vines = a naive host with none.
Total story: ~8-9 min.
:::
